section.title: The Paralytic and the Call of Matthew
section.sectionRationale: The miracles now provoke conflict. Jesus forgives and heals a paralytic, claiming an authority the scribes call blasphemy; He calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, scandalizing the Pharisees; and He answers a question about fasting by declaring Himself the bridegroom and His kingdom the new wine that cannot be poured into old skins. Grace and newness collide with religious resistance.
section.thesis: The Son of Man claims and proves the divine authority to forgive sins, comes as the physician of sinners who desires mercy rather than sacrifice, and reveals Himself as the bridegroom whose arrival brings a joy and newness that the old forms cannot contain.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the paralytic forgiven and healed; the call of Matthew; the meal with sinners and the word on mercy; and the question about fasting answered by the bridegroom, the patch, and the wineskins.

units.label: Your sins are forgiven
units.note: the Son of Man has authority

verses.text: Jesus got into a boat, crossed over, and came to His own town.
Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic lying on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are {{aphiemi|forgiven}}.”
On seeing this, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming!”
But Jesus knew what they were thinking and said, “Why do you harbor evil in your hearts?
Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has {{exousia|authority}} on earth to forgive sins...” Then He said to the paralytic, “Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
And the man got up and went home.
When the crowds saw this, they were filled with awe and glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
As Jesus went on from there, He saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Matthew got up and followed Him.
Later, as Jesus was dining at Matthew’s house, many tax collectors and sinners came and ate with Him and His disciples.
When the Pharisees saw this, they asked His disciples, “Why does your Teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
On hearing this, Jesus said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.
But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire {{eleos|mercy}}, not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to {{kaleo|call}} the righteous, but sinners.”

units.label: The bridegroom and the new wine

verses.text: Then John’s disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast so often, but Your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. For the patch will pull away from the garment, and a worse tear will result.

Neither do men pour new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins will burst, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

aphiemi.gloss: To send away, release, forgive. To forgive sins is to cancel the debt owed to God, which the scribes rightly know only God can do. Jesus' word to the paralytic is therefore a claim to divine authority, which He proves by the healing.

exousia.gloss: Authority, right, power. Jesus heals the paralytic so that all may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, tying the visible miracle to the invisible pardon as its proof.

eleos.gloss: Mercy, compassion, covenant kindness. Quoting Hosea 6:6, Jesus insists God desires mercy rather than mere ritual sacrifice; His table fellowship with sinners is not laxity but the very mercy God delights in.

kaleo.gloss: To call, summon, invite. Jesus came to call not the self-righteous but sinners; the word carries His gracious summons, the same call that lifted Matthew from the tax booth to discipleship.

basic.context: Back in Capernaum, friends bring a paralyzed man to Jesus, who startlingly forgives the man's sins first, then heals him to prove He has the authority to do so. He calls Matthew, a despised tax collector, and dines with tax collectors and sinners, drawing Pharisee criticism. Jesus answers that He is the doctor who came for the sick and desires mercy over sacrifice. When asked about fasting, He declares Himself the bridegroom whose presence brings joy and newness.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the paralytic scene as a deliberate claim to deity: the scribes are right that only God forgives sins, and Jesus proves His authority by the healing. Read the meal and the fasting question as revealing the character of His mission: mercy to sinners and a newness that cannot be patched onto the old. Each conflict sharpens the identity of Jesus.
basic.originalLanguages: To forgive is to cancel a debt owed to God, which is why the scribes cry blasphemy; Jesus claims that very authority and backs it with a miracle. He quotes Hosea: God desires mercy, not mere sacrifice. And He came to call sinners, the gracious summons that raised Matthew from his tax booth to follow Him.
basic.typology: Jesus as the divine forgiver fulfills the hope that God Himself would come to pardon His people. The bridegroom image draws on the Old Testament picture of God as the husband of Israel, now realized in Jesus. And the new wine signals the arrival of the new covenant that the old forms could not contain.
basic.christ: Jesus is revealed as the Son of Man who forgives sins with divine authority, the friend and physician of sinners, and the bridegroom whose coming is cause for joy. He is not adding a patch to old religion but bringing something gloriously new. And He is the one whose gracious call transforms a tax collector into a disciple and Gospel writer.
basic.god: God desires mercy, not mere ritual; He delights to forgive and to seek the sinful and the outcast. In Jesus, the God who alone can forgive draws near to pardon and heal. He is the God whose new covenant work has arrived, bringing a joy that the old wineskins of empty religion cannot hold.
basic.crossReferences: Hosea 6:6 is quoted, I desire mercy, not sacrifice. Isaiah 43 has God alone blotting out transgressions. 1 Timothy 1 says Christ came to save sinners, of whom Paul is chief. And Isaiah 62 pictures God rejoicing over His people as a bridegroom.
basic.oneStory: The King's mercy now meets open resistance, and the collision reveals who He is. He forgives sins as only God can, welcomes the very people religion despised, and announces that His coming is a wedding, not a funeral, bringing a newness the old forms cannot contain. The story moves forward as the friend of sinners gathers a people, even a tax collector, into the joy of His kingdom.

context.literary:
The passage is built as a chain of conflict stories in which each question from the opposition gives Jesus the chance to say who He is. Three groups raise objections in turn. Scribes object in their hearts to a word of forgiveness, verse 3. Pharisees object, speaking to the disciples, about the company He keeps, verse 11. John's disciples ask about fasting, verse 14. In each case Jesus answers with an image or a quotation and shows what He is: the one who forgives, the doctor who comes to the sick, the bridegroom who brings a feast.

The first scene has a notable break in the middle. In verse 6 Jesus begins a sentence, 'But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins...' and does not finish it. He turns instead to the paralytic and gives the command that completes the thought in action. The unfinished sentence leaves the reader to supply the ending, and the man's walking home is the grammar of the missing clause. Jesus has also framed the proof as a question: 'Which is easier?' Saying 'Your sins are forgiven' cannot be checked; saying 'Get up and walk' can. He chooses to do the harder, visible thing to prove the easier, invisible one.

The call of Matthew is one verse, and it is one of the briefest calls in the Gospel: 'Follow Me,' and he got up and followed. It is the hinge between the paralytic and the meal. The man who was told to get up does so, and so does the tax collector. Matthew himself is the next story, and he tells it without a word about his own feelings, in the third person, so that the focus is wholly on the call.

The passage ends with the pair of parables about cloth and wine, both drawn from the home. They explain the answer about fasting, and in a wider way they explain the whole run of scenes: something new has come that cannot simply be added to the old.
context.historical:
Capernaum was Jesus' base, 'His own town,' as Matthew calls it, and the scene takes place in a crowded house. Matthew leaves out the detail, given by Mark and Luke, that the friends lowered the man through the roof, Mark 2:4 and Luke 5:19. He keeps the spotlight on the forgiveness. In the first-century view, serious illness could be taken as a sign of God's displeasure, though Jesus will deny a simple link between a particular sin and a particular suffering, John 9:3, and the words 'your sins are forgiven' go to the root of what the man might have feared most.

A scribe's job was to interpret and apply the law, and the scribes in the house knew that God alone forgives sins, as Exodus 34:6 and 7 and Isaiah 43:25 teach. They were right about the principle. The priest could declare that a sacrifice had been accepted, and the prophet Nathan could tell David, 'The LORD has taken away your sin,' 2 Samuel 12:13, but neither of them pronounced forgiveness on his own authority. Jesus does. Blasphemy was a capital charge, and the same accusation is the one that the high priest will use against Him at His trial, Matthew 26:65.

Tax collectors gathered tolls and customs for the Roman authorities or their client rulers, and they were widely despised as collaborators who profited by overcharging. Capernaum was a town on a trade route, so a tax booth there makes good sense. Matthew's ordinary name 'Matthew' is joined in Mark and Luke by 'Levi,' Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27, and Matthew is the only Gospel writer who calls him 'the tax collector' in the list of the Twelve, Matthew 10:3.

To eat with someone in the ancient Near East was to accept them, and the Pharisees, who took great care over purity and who tithed even their herbs, Matthew 23:23, were scandalised that a rabbi would sit with those they counted as sinners. Fasting was a mark of serious piety. The only fast the law required was on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:29, but the Pharisees fasted twice a week, Luke 18:12, and John's disciples fasted too. Wineskins were made of animal hide. New wine still fermenting would stretch a new skin, while an old, stiffened skin would split.
context.canonical:
The story of the paralytic stands at the crossing of two Old Testament lines. One is that forgiveness is God's own act: 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake,' Isaiah 43:25, and 'To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness,' Daniel 9:9. The other is that sin and sickness appear together in the hope for the age to come. Psalm 103:3 praises the LORD, 'who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,' and Isaiah 33:24 promises that in Zion no one will say 'I am sick,' because the people 'will be forgiven of iniquity.' In Jesus the two come together in one word and one act.

The Hosea citation, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Hosea 6:6, belongs to the prophets' protest against religion without heart, Isaiah 1:11 to 17, Micah 6:6 to 8 and 1 Samuel 15:22. Jesus uses it twice, here and in Matthew 12:7, and in each case against those who put ritual before people. The Gospel's own teaching on mercy is gathered in Matthew 5:7 and 23:23.

The bridegroom image belongs to a long line in which the LORD is Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5 and 62:5, Jeremiah 2:2 and Hosea 2:19 and 20, and it carries on into the New Testament in John 3:29, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7 to 9. When Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, He takes a title that belonged to God.

The new wine speaks of the new covenant, 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:31 to 34, which Jesus names at the Last Supper, Luke 22:20, and which Hebrews 8:13 says makes the first obsolete.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew's readers were already being asked the questions of this passage by their neighbours. Is Jesus a blasphemer? Why does He keep such company? Why do His followers not keep the fasts? He wrote to give them answers, and each answer is a statement about Jesus.

To the first charge Matthew answers that the scribes had the principle right and the conclusion wrong. God alone forgives, and this is exactly what Jesus claims and proves. The 'authority on earth' is not the authority of a delegated priest but the Son of Man's own, and the crowd's praise of God who 'had given such authority to men' shows the first glimmer of what the church would later understand. Matthew expects readers to take the point that to receive forgiveness from Jesus is to receive it from God.

To the second charge, Matthew answers with Jesus' own words about the doctor and with Hosea, so that the reader sees that welcoming sinners is not a lapse from holiness but the heart of the Father's will. The listener is told, 'go and learn,' which is a rebuke to the learned: those who pride themselves on knowing the Scriptures have not yet understood what they say.

To the third, Matthew answers that the feast has come. The disciples of Jesus do not fast, because the bridegroom is present. The shadow of the cross is in the saying, but so is the promise of joy. Matthew also leaves the reader with the sharper point of the parables, that the kingdom is not an extra patch on a worn garment but a new thing that needs a new heart.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The events are described, and three lessons are drawn. The command to the paralytic, 'Get up, pick up your mat, and go home,' is specific to him, and the miracle is not a promise that every paralysed person will rise. The call, 'Follow Me,' is addressed to Matthew in particular, though the same word comes to every disciple. The quotation from Hosea, 'go and learn what this means,' is addressed to the Pharisees but belongs to all who read.

The saying about fasting does not say that Christians should not fast. Jesus says that after the bridegroom is taken away the guests will fast, verse 15, and He assumes in Matthew 6:16 to 18 that His followers will fast. What He denies is that fasting is a duty that must be performed in every circumstance by everyone as a sign of piety. The principle is that practice follows the season, and that no religious act should be allowed to contradict the presence of Christ.

The parables of the patch and the wineskins are not rules for sewing or storage, nor are they a plan for dismissing all that is old. They are pictures that explain why the kingdom's arrival changes how God's people live. What carries over is a call to receive what Christ gives on His terms, and a warning against trying to keep one's former religious life intact and add Jesus to it.

debates.question: Does Jesus' forgiving of sins amount to a claim to be God?

views.label: Yes, He exercises a prerogative that is God's alone
views.case: The scribes are right that forgiveness belongs to God, Isaiah 43:25 and Mark 2:7, and Jesus does not correct their principle. He answers by showing that He knows their hearts, which is also a divine capacity, 1 Kings 8:39, and by doing a visible miracle to demonstrate His right. Later the same charge of blasphemy is brought at His trial, Matthew 26:65, and John says the Jews sought to kill Him for making Himself equal with God, John 5:18.

views.label: He acts as the Son of Man to whom God has given authority
views.case: Jesus speaks of 'the Son of Man' who 'has authority on earth' to forgive, the figure of Daniel 7:13 and 14 who is given dominion. The crowd praises God 'who had given such authority to men,' verse 8. On this view Jesus acts as God's authorised agent. The authority is received, though it is one that no mere prophet could hold.

debates.bearing: The two views need not conflict. Jesus claims an authority that He says is His on earth, and that authority is exactly what the Old Testament reserves for God. The reader has to decide who He must be.

debates.question: Did the paralytic's sin cause his paralysis?

views.label: Jesus is not saying that this man's sin caused his illness
views.case: He treats forgiveness and healing as separate gifts, and elsewhere He explicitly denies that a particular disability is the result of a particular sin, John 9:3. The man's deepest need is forgiveness, and the healing is the visible sign that it has been granted.

views.label: Illness and sin are bound together in a fallen world
views.case: Scripture sees sickness as part of the order damaged by sin, and passages such as Psalm 103:3 and Isaiah 33:24 link forgiveness with healing. Jesus' words speak to the man's own sense that the two were connected, and His healing shows the reversal of both.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage does not allow us to blame sufferers for their illness. It shows that the root problem is sin and that Jesus deals with that first, before the symptom.

debates.question: What do the patch and the wineskins teach about the old order?

views.label: The kingdom brings a newness that cannot be added to old forms
views.case: Jesus is not offering a mend for the existing system of Pharisaic piety. The new wine of the kingdom needs new skins, and the attempt to hold it in the old will destroy both. His disciples' joy cannot be fitted into a regime of fasts and traditions.

views.label: Fulfilment, not rejection, of the Law and the Prophets
views.case: Jesus has said that He has not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it, Matthew 5:17, and the Old Testament itself promised the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:31. The parables target brittle human traditions and show that grace needs hearts that are renewed to hold it.

debates.bearing: Both agree that Jesus brings something new from God that requires transformed hearts. The newness fulfils the old promises rather than rejecting them.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to the paralytic is tharsei, 'take courage,' joined to teknon, 'child.' Matthew uses tharseo only a few times, and each time it is on Jesus' lips, to a paralysed man here, to the woman with a flow of blood, 9:22, and to the frightened disciples on the sea, 14:27, where it is followed by 'It is I.' It is a word for the settled courage that comes from a presence. The title 'child' is a tender one for a grown man, and it opens the way to the forgiveness that follows.

The scribes say that Jesus blasphemei, 'blasphemes,' verse 3, from blasphemeo, to speak against God. The charge assumes that Jesus is a man, claiming a right that belongs to God alone. When the high priest uses the same verb at the trial, Matthew 26:65, the reader sees that the whole Gospel turns on whether the charge is right. In verse 4 Jesus knows their thoughts, and there is a textual note: the BSB footnote says that NA, BYZ and TR read 'saw' rather than 'knew,' so that either way the point is that He perceived what they had not spoken.

The command 'Get up' is egeire, from egeiro, the verb that Matthew uses of the resurrection, 'He has risen,' egerthe, 28:6. The same verb is used again for the man who 'got up,' verse 7. The crowds' response is that they were phobeo, afraid, which the BSB softens to 'filled with awe,' and the fear is the right reverence of those who have met God at work.

Matthew sits at the telonion, the tax booth, and is a telones, a tax collector. The word joins with hamartoloi, 'sinners,' in verse 10 and in Luke 15:1, a pairing that describes a class judged to be outside the covenant. Jesus' call is akolouthei moi, 'Follow Me,' in the present tense of command, and Matthew's response is anastas ekolouthesen, 'he arose and followed,' a quick aorist pair, with no hesitation.

In verse 12 the 'healthy' are hoi ischuontes, literally 'the strong,' and the sick are hoi kakos echontes, 'those who have it badly,' and the doctor is iatros. Jesus then says that He came to call the righteous 'not,' where the BSB footnote points out that some manuscripts add 'to repentance,' as in Luke 5:32. Hosea 6:6 in Hebrew has chesed, 'loyal love,' where the Greek Old Testament and Matthew have eleos.

The disciples of John ask why they fast polla, 'often'; the BSB footnote says some editions omit it. Jesus calls the wedding guests 'the sons of the bridal chamber,' huioi tou nymphonos, and says the bridegroom will be taken away, from apairo, a verb that some hear as an allusion to Isaiah 53:8, 'He was taken away.' The patch is agnaphos, cloth not yet shrunk by washing. And while the wine is neos, 'young, fresh,' the skins that can hold it are kainos, 'new in kind,' the same word as in the 'new covenant,' Luke 22:20.

typology.type: The God who forgives sins in person
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament never allowed any human being to forgive sin as of right. The LORD is the one who 'blots out your transgressions for My own sake,' Isaiah 43:25, and a prophet like Nathan could say only that the LORD had taken the sin away, 2 Samuel 12:13. In Jesus the forgiver is present in a body, and says 'your sins are forgiven' in His own name. The correspondence is that forgiveness comes from God; the escalation is that He speaks it in person and proves it by a sign. The fullest form of the forgiveness comes at the cross, 'the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28, and Paul says God 'canceled the debt ascribed to us' by 'nailing it to the cross,' Colossians 2:14. The type falls short in that the healing of a paralytic is a sign and not yet the whole of salvation.

The LORD was Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5, who rejoices over His people as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, Isaiah 62:5, and who pledged Himself in covenant, Ezekiel 16:8 and Hosea 2:19 and 20. When Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, He takes this role. John the Baptist already speaks of himself as the friend of the bridegroom, John 3:29. Paul sees the church as the bride for whom Christ gave Himself, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and the Revelation ends with the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7 to 9. The type falls short of its goal only in time: the bridegroom is still to be 'taken away' and to return, and the wedding feast is not yet fully come.

typology.type: The new wine and the new covenant
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah promised a covenant unlike the old, with the law written on hearts and sins remembered no more, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34. The Gospels connect that covenant to Jesus' blood, Matthew 26:28 and Luke 22:20. The new wine of the kingdom is that covenant's life and joy, and it cannot be held in the brittle forms of a religion based on outward observance. The fulfilment comes in the gift of the Spirit and the new heart, which Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 had promised. The picture falls short if it is read as a rejection of the Old Testament: Hebrews 8:13 says that the first covenant is made obsolete, and yet the same author uses that covenant's sacrifices to explain Christ's own.

The LORD describes Himself as the healer of His people, Exodus 15:26, and the psalmist praises Him as the one who 'forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,' Psalm 103:3. In Matthew 9, Jesus says, 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick,' and acts in that role by touching, calling and eating with the sick. The correspondence is that God has always been the healer of His people. The escalation is that He now seeks the sick in their homes and tax booths. The picture falls short in that the self-righteous are also sick, and Jesus says so by the very form of His saying: those who think they are well will not call for the doctor.

study.christ:
The passage unveils Jesus in three ways, each of which is a claim that He makes and a claim He backs.

He is the Son of Man who forgives sins. Matthew has told us at the start that He will 'save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, and the first man in Matthew 9 receives exactly that. The order of the story is the Gospel in miniature: before anything is said about his body, the man is told that his sins are forgiven. Jesus then proves what He has said by what can be seen. He does not argue for His authority; He demonstrates it, and He makes the proof depend on the question of which is easier. The visible healing is a promissory note for the invisible forgiveness. The cross and the resurrection are where that note is fully paid: His blood is 'poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28.

He is the friend of sinners and the doctor who comes to the sick. His mission is described in the words 'I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,' and elsewhere, 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,' Luke 19:10. Matthew's own call is the first proof. The man at the tax booth was beyond respectable hope, and is now named in the list of the Twelve, with his old trade still attached to his name, Matthew 10:3. Jesus is not afraid of defilement, because His holiness heals what it touches, as it did with the leper in chapter 8.

He is the bridegroom. By accepting the name that the prophets gave to the LORD, He announces that His coming is the beginning of the wedding. This is why the presence of Jesus is a time for feasting, and why He promises that the time of His absence, when He is 'taken away,' will be a time of fasting. In a phrase the whole of the Gospel's storyline is told: joy, death, absence, return.

As a caution, the passage does not ask us to find Christ in every detail of the roof, the mat or the cloth. The parables of the patch and the skins are pictures meant to make a single point, that the kingdom is new. The links above rest on the passage's own claims and on the way the New Testament uses the Old.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He delights to forgive. The scribes' principle is right: only God forgives. But their assumption is that He does so from a distance and after due process. Jesus shows a God who forgives first, in a house full of people, without any ritual, to a man who has asked for nothing but healing. The long tradition behind this is in Exodus 34:6 and 7, where the LORD declares Himself 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion,' and in Micah 7:18, 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity... because He delights in loving devotion?'

The passage shows a God who wants mercy more than ritual. 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' is no rejection of the sacrifices that He commanded; Hosea speaks within a tradition in which the sacrifices were the means of grace. It is a protest against any religion that keeps the forms and loses the heart, as Isaiah 1:11 to 17 and Psalm 51:16 and 17 also say. The God of Israel is a God who looks for compassion, and who rebukes the learned for not knowing the meaning of their own Bible.

He is a God who knows hearts. Jesus 'knew what they were thinking,' and the Old Testament says that the LORD alone knows the hearts of all, 1 Kings 8:39 and Jeremiah 17:10. His knowledge is not used to condemn the scribes at once but to give them a chance to see. He asks, 'Why do you harbor evil in your hearts?'

He is a God who rejoices in His people like a bridegroom. This is one of the warmest pictures of God in the Bible. The one who made them delights in them, Isaiah 62:5, and the arrival of the Son is the arrival of the feast. The same God is also holy, and the sense of the bridegroom's departure is a reminder that joy is bought at a price.

For worship, the passage teaches us to come as the paralytic and his friends did, with faith that carries a burden to Jesus. We come as Matthew did, answering a call with all that we have, and as the guests at the table do, glad to be there. The right response to a forgiving God is not fear but the awe of the crowd, who 'glorified God.'

crossReferences.note: Mark tells the same story with the detail of the roof opened and the man lowered, and adds the scribes' question, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' The question sets out in plain words what Matthew leaves for the reader to see: that forgiveness is God's act, and that Jesus claims it.

God says, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more.' The doubled 'I' stresses that forgiveness is God's own work. It is this text that makes the scribes' reaction in Matthew 9:3 intelligible, and it makes Jesus' claim all the more striking.

The psalmist praises the LORD 'who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.' The two benefits come together in this verse and in Matthew 9, where Jesus forgives and heals in a single scene. It shows that the miracle completes the forgiveness and is not a separate thing.

When David confesses, Nathan says, 'The LORD has taken away your sin.' The prophet announces that God has forgiven, and does not do it in his own name. That is the contrast with Jesus, who says, 'your sins are forgiven,' and who therefore does what no prophet had done.

'For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' Hosea speaks to a people whose love vanishes like the morning mist, and the verse pairs mercy with the knowledge of God. Jesus quotes it to say that those who truly know God will be merciful to sinners.

The tax collectors and sinners gather to listen to Jesus, and the Pharisees grumble that He welcomes them and eats with them. The shepherd's search for the one lost sheep is Jesus' answer, and the same joy of heaven appears over one repentant sinner, which shows the heart of the mission described in Matthew 9:13.

'As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.' It is one of the central places where the LORD is the bridegroom of His people. When Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom in Matthew 9:15, He takes the place of the LORD in this image.

The promise of a new covenant, with the law written on hearts and sins forgiven and remembered no more. The new wine of Matthew 9:17 is the life of this covenant, and the forgiveness Jesus gives to the paralytic is the heart of what Jeremiah promised.

Luke names the tax collector Levi, and adds that he left everything, held a great banquet in his house, and that Jesus' reply ends with 'to repentance.' It fills out Matthew's brief account and shows what the 'getting up' of Matthew 9:9 cost.

'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst.' Paul's own testimony restates the mission in Matthew 9:13. He too was called from an unlikely place, and he sees in his own case the pattern of the Lord's mercy.

The marriage of the Lamb has come, and those invited to the supper are blessed. It is the final fulfilment of the bridegroom's word in Matthew 9:15: the time of the guests' mourning gives way to a feast that does not end.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man and a woman who hid from God because of what they had done, Genesis 3:8, and the rest of the story is God's search for them. Among all the things that sin broke, the first and worst was the nearness between God and His people. In Matthew 9 the one who made that nearness possible is standing in a house in Capernaum, and the first thing He does for a broken man is to speak the words that the whole Old Testament was waiting for: your sins are forgiven.

The Old Testament's answer to sin was the sacrificial system, with its priests, blood and Day of Atonement. It showed the seriousness of sin and gave a way of approach, but its sacrifices could never put sin away, as Hebrews 10:4 says. The prophets saw further. They said that God desired mercy and not sacrifice, that He would make a new covenant and forgive iniquity, Jeremiah 31:34, and that His Servant would bear the sin of many, Isaiah 53:12. Matthew shows how those promises begin to arrive: the forgiver is here, He eats with sinners, and He has a name for Himself that belongs to the LORD.

The call of Matthew also takes us into the story of how God gathers a people. Abraham was called out of Ur, and Israel out of Egypt. Now a tax collector is called out of the toll booth, and with him the Gospel signals that the net is cast wide. The one who sat at the booth becomes one of the Twelve and, according to tradition, the author of this very book, though the Gospel itself does not say so. What the story makes plain is that no one is beyond the call.

The bridegroom's words point to the end. The time of the guests' joy will give way to a time of fasting when He is taken away, and Matthew's readers know that this means the cross, Matthew 26:2 and 27:35. But the story does not stop at the grave. The marriage supper of the Lamb will come, Revelation 19:9, and the new Jerusalem will appear 'as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. Everything that began with a man hiding in a garden ends with a people at a feast, forgiven, healed and welcomed by the bridegroom Himself.

quiz.q: Why did the scribes accuse Jesus of blasphemy when He spoke to the paralytic?

options.text: Because He claimed to forgive sins, which they knew only God can do.
options.note: Verses 2-3 show the offense: Jesus exercised a divine prerogative in pardoning sins.

options.text: Because He healed a man on the Sabbath.
options.note: That is a different conflict; here the offense was His claim to forgive sins.

options.text: Because He touched an unclean paralytic.
options.note: The charge concerned forgiving sins, not ritual uncleanness.

options.text: Because He refused to heal the man at all.
options.note: He did heal him; the offense was His prior claim to forgive sins.

quiz.q: How did Jesus prove His authority to forgive sins?

options.text: By healing the paralytic, a visible act showing His authority over the invisible one.
options.note: Verse 6 ties the healing to proving the Son of Man's authority to forgive.

options.text: By quoting Scripture to silence the scribes.
options.note: He did reason with them, but the proof He offered was the healing itself.

options.text: By calling down fire from heaven.
options.note: No such sign occurs; He healed the man as proof.

options.text: By simply insisting louder that He had the right.
options.note: He gave a real demonstration, the healing, not mere insistence.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus eat with tax collectors and sinners?

options.text: Because He came as a physician for the sick, to call sinners, desiring mercy over sacrifice.
options.note: Verses 12-13 give His reason: mercy and the call of sinners.

options.text: Because He wanted to enjoy their company and hospitality.
options.note: There was real fellowship, but His stated purpose was to seek and call sinners, not mere socializing.

options.text: Because He approved of their dishonest practices.
options.note: He called them as sinners needing mercy, not because He approved of their sin.

options.text: Because He had given up on the religious leaders entirely.
options.note: His point was the nature of His mission to sinners, not abandoning anyone out of spite.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer the question about why His disciples did not fast?

options.text: The guests do not mourn while the bridegroom is present; His coming brings joy.
options.note: Verse 15 pictures Jesus as the bridegroom whose presence is cause for celebration.

options.text: Fasting is never appropriate for His followers.
options.note: He says they will fast when the bridegroom is taken away, so fasting has its time; this overstates.

options.text: His disciples were simply not devout enough to fast.
options.note: The reason is the bridegroom's presence, not any lack of devotion.

options.text: Fasting had been abolished by the law of Moses.
options.note: The law did not abolish fasting; Jesus points to the joy of His presence.

quiz.q: What do the patch and the wineskins illustrate?

options.text: The newness of Jesus' kingdom cannot be contained by the old, brittle forms.
options.note: Verses 16-17 show the new wine of the kingdom requires new wineskins.

options.text: That believers should discard everything from the Old Testament.
options.note: Jesus fulfills rather than discards the Law and Prophets; the images target rigid, self-righteous forms.

options.text: That old traditions are always better than new ones.
options.note: The point is the opposite; the new wine needs new skins to hold it.

options.text: That Jesus came to make no changes at all.
options.note: The imagery announces a genuinely new work that the old forms cannot hold.

questions: Jesus addressed the paralytic's deepest need, forgiveness, before his obvious need of healing. What surface need are you focused on, and what deeper need might Jesus want to meet first?
Matthew got up from his tax booth and followed at a word. Is there something Jesus is calling you to leave behind in order to follow Him more fully?
Jesus said He desires mercy, not sacrifice, and welcomed sinners to His table. Who are the people your circles tend to exclude, and how might you show them the mercy Jesus shows?
The Pharisees were scandalized that Jesus ate with sinners. Do you ever resent grace being shown to people you think do not deserve it, and how does your own need of mercy reframe that?
Jesus is the bridegroom whose presence turns fasting into feasting. How does knowing Him as a source of deep joy, not just duty, change the way you follow Him?

translationNotes.note: The sentence breaks off mid-thought, so that you may know the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, then turns to command the healing; the interrupted grammar dramatizes the proof about to be given.
I desire mercy, not sacrifice quotes Hosea 6:6; some later manuscripts add to repentance after but sinners, as the BSB footnote notes.
Wineskins were animal hides; new wine still fermenting would stretch and burst old, brittle skins, illustrating the incompatibility of the kingdom's newness with rigid old forms.
